questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5\end{aligned}]
$$

given that the general solution to our differential equation is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The solution to the initial value problem is

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{t}+\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{-t}.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} |  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
To find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=5 \\ {c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the result to the second equation, we get

$$
5{c}_{1}=5\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2\cdot 1+{c}_{2}=5\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=3.
$$

 
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=7$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2} \\ -{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}=6 \\ -{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second equation by $-1$ and adding the result to the first equation, we get

$$
{c}_{2}=6.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-{c}_{1}+4\cdot 6=6\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=18.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =18\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+6\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(7)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(7) & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\cdot 7}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{28}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18{e}^{28}+24{e}^{-7} \\ -18{e}^{28}+18{e}^{-7}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=2$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=3 \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
4{c}_{1}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-1+{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=4.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(2)}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(2)} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{6} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4}+4{e}^{6} \\ 5{e}^{-4}-4{e}^{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=5 \\ 2{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ -2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=3 \\ -2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the result to the second equation, we get

$$
6{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ 4{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2 \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}

Subtracting the first equation from the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}=-3\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=-1.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}-1+{c}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}

$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=1$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 2{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-2{e}^{4} \\ 2{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}={e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3}{c}_{1}=3{e}^{4}\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=e.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=e$ into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3}(e)+{c}_{2}={e}^{4}\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-{e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =e[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-{e}^{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Let $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-2$ be eigenvalues of the $2\times 2$ matrix  $A$ that correspond to eigenvectors 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/15d8764ce12b985a991ca9a0704ba037ccc29fa488a3f23ee643688ceebae60c.png) 
Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $\mathbf{x}(t)$ and that $\mathbf{x}(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/88cd1c87501899a5d6b49ce3fd1678fe9485300a2da638fb496f2c80b298ea86.png)
find the position of the particle after $2$ seconds.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\color{red}\lambda_1}, {\color{blue}\lambda_2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2,$ we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ -2{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-11 \\ -2{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $3$ and adding the result to the second equation, we get

$$
16c_1 = -32
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
c_1=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-2\cdot(-2) -3c_2 = 1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
c_2=1.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $\mathbf x(2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\cdot 2}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2\cdot 2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12{e}^{6}+{e}^{-4} \\ 4{e}^{6}-3{e}^{-4}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
\lambda_1= 2

\lambda_2= -3.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1 =2,$ we get

- For $\lambda_2 =-3,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/704493d5ac4f48c88a9c521c4e43c41acfd80b6d6959237944fbc0d638e6012f.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/a77312d93a804e69dabb70aff5bc7bbf9798781c728dfc50fff1440da86b5b5c.png)

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2,$ we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution and use the initial values:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=5 \\ {c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{c}_{2}=-5\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $c_2 = -1$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-1=5\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =6[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$
